name: Emeka Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Emeka, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company that records water-quality samples for local utilities. I have a bachelor’s degree and can fix ordinary data problems, but I call the sampling crew when a reading looks impossible. I compare the bottle label, the collection time and the report that goes to the utility. I use AI now and then to draft a test, then check the sample trail myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else depends on the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lila teaches paid dance classes, with bookings that change by season, and our children are grown. My pay is typical for a developer and carries most of our mortgage. We have about five months of expenses saved, and some other software jobs nearby. Retirement is not far away, but we have not confirmed what personal income we could actually rely on then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the utility AI Plateau still leaves us checking the bottle and the result. A clean report does not tell you who filled the sample jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my salary and the mortgage are secure in this picture. Lila’s class bookings rise and fall, but five months saved can bridge a slow term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing sample labels with collection times and have the crew confirm doubtful readings. I’d continue saving 200 monthly while my wage holds. In the first year I’d use AI only on invented sample data, not the utility’s private site records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household income. I still dislike a report that looks certain when the bottle label is smudged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which sample label raised doubt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A jar arrived with the right site number but the wrong collection date. The crew remembered that road was closed, which made us check the date again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do dance fees enter the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila and I would keep her class fees for everyday extras, not for the fixed mortgage payment. I would not promise our children gifts based on a future retirement figure.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking water samples.
I would match **bottle labels** with collection times.
think: I expect my **developer salary** to cover the mortgage while sample records still need checking.
Our **five-month reserve** bridges slow dance-class terms without missing regular housing bills.
do: **Compare** sample labels, times and crew reports.
**Use** AI only with invented samples, not private site records.
feel: **Calm** about income, wary of uncertain sample labels.
S0.quote: A clean report does not tell you who filled the sample jar.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** stays on invented data while field crews resolve doubtful samples.
A stable main wage and **five months saved** absorb seasonal class bookings.

steps.text: Keep checking water sample labels and times with field crews
Save 200 monthly while developer pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check sample code before robots collect water. I would ask the staff union to protect a human check when a water alert could close a public tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our company could reduce testing hours, including mine. Five months saved gives me time to look, but Lila’s bookings could also fall if families cut extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the union’s water-data group and bring three anonymised sample-mix cases. I’d ask the sampling crew to check an AI-generated alert against its bottle chain before it goes live. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d search actual utility data posts with written pay that, with Lila’s usual class income, covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though the reserve buys time. I do not want a false alert to make a neighbourhood fear its water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mixed sample belongs in the union case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One sample had a high result because two jars were swapped in the van. I would take that case to the group without naming the crew member.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lila add classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila would keep teaching classes actually booked. We would not count a spring timetable as paid work until families enrol.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach water-data code before sample-collection robots.
I would demand **human alert checks** through the union.
think: I expect my **testing hours** could shrink as AI handles routine water-data checks.
I worry **dance bookings** could fall as families cut extras during the same period.
do: **Join** union water-data group with three anonymous sample cases.
**Require** crew review of AI alerts against bottle chains.
**Search** real utility posts if hours fall, with stated pay plus Lila’s usual bookings covering our mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible reduced hours, with five months to search.
S1.quote: I do not want a false alert to make a neighbourhood fear its water.
fieldNote: His **union case** uses anonymised jar swaps and calls for a crew check before alerts.
A **job search** starts if his hours fall, with written household-covering pay.

steps.text: Join union group with three anonymous water-sample cases and demand crew-checked alerts
Search actual utility posts if hours fall only with pay covering mortgage alongside usual class income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches our data and coding work in 2028; hands-on water-sampling robots follow around 2031. The collection route may still need people for a while, but scheduling changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer job may be cut. Five months saved lets us make choices, yet other software firms may stop hiring the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and keep our reserve against the mortgage. I’d ask the union to bargain as a group for a named human on disputed water results. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help, without counting future dance bookings or our children’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my main wage, and I would sleep badly if we had no paid opening. Five months of savings is time to search, not a replacement salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the household can manage for some months. I would not ask them to cover a mortgage before they can cover their own rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would sampling crews hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the field crew whether it still has paid posts. A later robot date does not guarantee that a sampling company will hire me.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach code before 2031 sampling robots.
I would demand **human result appeals** after software cuts.
think: I expect my **developer job** could be cut.
I cannot assume **other software firms** keep hiring under full AGI.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and reserve mortgage cash.
**Bargain** through union for named humans on disputed water results.
**Apply** for real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the main wage despite five months saved.
S2.quote: Five months of savings is time to search, not a replacement salary.
fieldNote: His **2028 code risk** precedes physical sampling robots around 2031 and threatens the main mortgage-paying wage.
The **five-month reserve** buys time; union bargaining starts now, while job applications and eligible help follow displacement.

steps.text: Bargain through union for named human review of disputed water results
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches code in 2031 and water-sampling robots around 2034. Five years might let me learn to collect and document a physical sample, but I would check who is hiring first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think code work could shrink. I know the software record, not the whole field procedure, and a volunteer visit would not pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the local water cooperative for permission to shadow a field sampler on my day off, using its safety gear and training. I’d do it only if the cooperative provides the equipment and a supervisor, without costing paid developer hours or our reserve. In the first year after 2031, if code ends, I’d apply only to a real paid sampling vacancy that still hires people despite 2034 robots and whose wage with Lila’s usual booked classes covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code pay, with time for a limited field test. I will not buy safety gear for a vacancy that has not been advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with a physical sample?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A technician showed me how a loose cap can ruin a sample before the lab sees it. I would need supervised practice in sealing and recording the jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which dance classes count in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila’s usual booked classes would go into the wage comparison. We would not count a possible summer workshop unless someone has paid for it.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 sampling robots.
I would test **supervised field work** before seeking a paid sampling post.
think: I expect **code work** could shrink when full thinking AI arrives in 2031.
I know **volunteer field time** cannot replace the wage that covers most mortgage payments.
do: **Shadow** sampler only with cooperative gear, supervisor and no lost developer pay.
**Practise** sealing and logging jars without spending the household reserve.
**Apply** if coding ends after 2031 only to still-hiring sampling posts with pay plus Lila’s usual booked classes covering mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about code income, with a bounded field test.
S3.quote: I will not buy safety gear for a vacancy that has not been advertised.
fieldNote: His **field learning** requires cooperative permission, supplied safety gear, supervision and no lost paid time.
A **sampling transition** needs a real post, continued hiring and enough pay with Lila’s usual classes.

steps.text: Shadow sampler only with permission, free gear, supervision and no lost pay or savings
Apply after 2031 coding loss only to hiring sampling jobs with mortgage-covering pay plus booked classes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches water-data code in 2036; hands-on sampling robots follow around 2039. A decade allows measured paid transitions and an honest look at retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage is safe now, though testing hours could narrow before 2036. I will not guess a pension amount or use the children’s wages to fill a hole in our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking bottle records with crews and save 200 monthly while my wage holds. I’d ask the union each year for the number of funded field places and lost data hours. In the first year after 2036, if code ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income, savings and mortgage figures show we can cover ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later testing jobs, with today’s mortgage affordable. I can use the decade to ask for actual figures rather than a reassuring story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request our retirement statements and compare them with the mortgage balance. Lila’s classes are paid by bookings, not by a promise on a course calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should funded transitions count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to count paid field jobs filled, not just people who attended a workshop. A certificate without wages leaves the mortgage where it was.

I would demand **funded field places** with actual paid jobs.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold while people still check water results.
I worry **testing hours** could narrow before the full 2036 change arrives.

feel: **Uneasy** about future hours, with current mortgage security.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the main wage could end before a field route is even tested. Written terms, human water-result appeals, eligible help and a paid opening would help. Five months saved lets us act but does not let us retire.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the sampler what happened to the bottle between the stream and the report. A number without a chain of custody is only a guess.

headlineQuote: A number without a chain of custody is only a guess.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and five months saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** but checks water records against physical bottle labels and field crews.
His partner’s **dance-class income** varies; his wage carries most of their mortgage.
He explores **supervised sampling** only with cooperative gear, no lost pay, real vacancies and sufficient household wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end the main wage before a field path is tested.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, human result appeals, eligible help and a paid opening would help.
